sourceReference: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, Chapter 3, Problem 112
title: 100-meter Race Time Analysis
statement: In a 100-m race, the winner is timed at 11.2 s. The second-place finisher's time is 11.6 s. How far is the second-place finisher behind the winner when she crosses the finish line? Assume the velocity of each runner is constant throughout the race.

solution.approach: Find each runner's constant velocity, then calculate how far the second-place finisher has traveled when the winner finishes.

steps.description: Find how far the second-place finisher has traveled when the winner finishes
Calculate how far behind the second-place finisher is

hints.hint: Think about what constant velocity means and how to calculate it from distance and time.
Calculate each runner's velocity first, then find how far the second runner has gone when the first runner finishes.
Use v = d/t for each runner, then multiply the second runner's velocity by the winner's time to find their position.

problemSpecificErrors.error: Using the second runner's time instead of the winner's time
problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student calculates distance based on 11.6 s instead of 11.2 s
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: Remember, we want to know where the second runner is when the winner finishes, so use the winner's time (11.2 s).
The question asks for distance, not time. You need to find positions at the same moment in time.

sourceReference: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, Chapter 3, Problem 113
title: Position Function Analysis
statement: The position of a particle moving along the x-axis varies with time according to x(t) = 5.0t² - 4.0t³ m. Find (a) the velocity and acceleration of the particle as functions of time, (b) the velocity and acceleration at t = 2.0 s, (c) the time at which the position is a maximum, (d) the time at which the velocity is zero, and (e) the maximum position.

solution.approach: Use calculus: velocity is the first derivative of position, acceleration is the second derivative. Set velocity to zero to find extrema.

steps.description: Find velocity by taking the first derivative of position
Find acceleration by taking the derivative of velocity

steps.explanation: Maximum occurs at t = 0.833 s (where v = 0 and this represents a maximum)

hints.hint: Remember that velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time, and acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
Use the power rule for derivatives: d/dt(t^n) = nt^(n-1). Set v(t) = 0 to find when the particle momentarily stops.
For part (a): v(t) = d/dt(5.0t² - 4.0t³) = 10.0t - 12.0t². For the maximum, solve 10.0t - 12.0t² = 0.

problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student gets wrong coefficients in v(t) or a(t)
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: Remember the power rule: d/dt(at^n) = nat^(n-1). Double-check your derivative calculations.

problemSpecificErrors.error: Not recognizing that t = 0 is also a solution
problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student only finds t = 0.833 s when velocity is zero
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: When you factor out t from t(10.0 - 12.0t) = 0, remember that t = 0 is also a solution.

problemSpecificErrors.error: Using wrong time for maximum position
problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student uses t = 0 instead of t = 0.833 s
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: The maximum position occurs where the particle momentarily stops moving (v = 0) at t = 0.833 s, not at t = 0.

sourceReference: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, Chapter 3, Problem 114
title: Cyclist Sprint Analysis
statement: A cyclist sprints at the end of a race to clinch a victory. She has an initial velocity of 11.5 m/s and accelerates at a rate of 0.500 m/s² for 7.00 s. (a) What is her final velocity? (b) The cyclist continues at this velocity to the finish line. If she is 300 m from the finish line when she starts to accelerate, how much time did she save? (c) The second-place winner was 5.00 m ahead when the winner started to accelerate, but he was unable to accelerate, and traveled at 11.8 m/s until the finish line. What was the difference in finish time in seconds between the winner and runner-up? How far back was the runner-up when the winner crossed the finish line?

givenValues.description: Distance from finish when acceleration starts

solution.approach: Use kinematic equations for accelerated motion, then analyze constant velocity motion. Compare times for both scenarios.

steps.description: Find time for remaining distance at constant velocity

steps.explanation: Runner starts 5.00 m ahead, so travels 305 m total

steps.description: Find how far back runner-up is when winner finishes

finalAnswer.text: (a) 15.0 m/s; (b) 5.3 s; (c) 5.0 s difference, 59.6 m behind

hints.hint: Break this into phases: acceleration phase and constant velocity phase. Use kinematic equations for each.
For part (a), use v = v₀ + at. For part (b), compare total time with and without acceleration. For part (c), track both runners' positions.
During acceleration: x = v₀t + ½at². Then find remaining distance and time at constant velocity. The second runner starts 5 m ahead, so travels 305 m total.

problemSpecificErrors.error: Forgetting the initial 5 m lead for the second runner
problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student calculates second runner traveling 300 m instead of 305 m
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: Remember that the second-place runner was 5.00 m ahead when the winner started accelerating, so they need to travel 305 m total.

problemSpecificErrors.error: Not accounting for both phases of the winner's motion
problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student only considers either acceleration or constant velocity phase
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: The winner's motion has two phases: 7 seconds of acceleration, then constant velocity for the remaining distance.

problemSpecificErrors.error: Incorrect calculation of distance during acceleration
problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student uses x = vt instead of x = v₀t + ½at²
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: During acceleration, use the full kinematic equation x = v₀t + ½at², not just x = vt.

sourceReference: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, Chapter 3, Problem 115
title: Motorcycle World Record Analysis
statement: In 1967, New Zealander Burt Munro set the world record for an Indian motorcycle, on the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, of 295.38 km/h. The one-way course was 8.00 km long. Acceleration rates are often described by the time it takes to reach 96.0 km/h from rest. If this time was 4.00 s and Burt accelerated at this rate until he reached his maximum speed, how long did it take Burt to complete the course?

solution.approach: Find the acceleration rate, calculate time and distance to reach maximum speed, then add time for constant velocity phase.

steps.description: Find time to reach maximum speed
Find remaining distance at constant speed
Find time for constant speed phase

hints.hint: First find the acceleration rate from the given information about reaching 96.0 km/h in 4.00 s.
Use this acceleration to find how long it takes to reach maximum speed, then calculate the distance covered during acceleration.
The motion has two phases: acceleration to max speed, then constant speed. Find the time for each phase and add them together.

problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student doesn't convert km/h to m/s or uses wrong conversion factor
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: Remember to convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by (1000 m/km)/(3600 s/h) = 5/18.

problemSpecificErrors.error: Using wrong kinematic equation for acceleration distance
problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student uses x = vt instead of x = ½at² or x = v₀t + ½at²
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: For motion from rest with constant acceleration, use x = ½at² to find the distance.

problemSpecificErrors.howToDetect: Student calculates total time as 8000 m / 82.05 m/s
problemSpecificErrors.feedback: Burt doesn't travel at maximum speed for the entire course - he must accelerate first, which takes time and distance.
